title: The days of tashriq
hookLine: days of eating, drinking and remembrance in Mina (Muslim)

lines: REMEMBER GOD AS YOU REMEMBERED THEM.
cards: When the pilgrimage was over, in the days before Islam, people would gather and talk about their fathers: whose ancestor fed the most guests, whose clan had the proudest name.
That's the scene commentators on the Qur'an give for a verse in Surah Al-Baqarah: when the rites are done, remember God as you used to remember your fathers, or with a stronger remembrance.
Same gathering, same tents, same food. A different name on everyone's lips. Today, the days of tashriq.

teach.b: After the day of sacrifice, the pilgrims go back down to Mina and stay. These are the days of tashriq. First, what they're for.
In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says the days of tashriq are days of eating and drinking, and in one wording, of remembering God.
You met that saying back on day five hundred fourteen, at Eid. Not fasting days, scholars conclude. Feast days.
Food is part of the worship here, not a break from it. Second, the counted days.

Surah Al-Baqarah tells the pilgrims to remember God through the appointed days, then offers a choice: whoever hurries off after two days, no sin on him, and whoever stays on, no sin on him either, for the one who is mindful of God.
Two good ways out; the condition the verse names is mindfulness, not the schedule. Third, the stones again.

Aisha describes, in Sunan Abi Dawud, how the Prophet stayed at Mina those nights and stoned the pillars each day after noon, a takbir with each pebble. At the first two pillars, she says, he stood a long time in du'a.
At the last, he didn't stop.

teach.h: A LONG STAND AT THE PILLARS.
teach.b: So the days hold a rhythm: a meal, a walk to the pillars, a long stand, a meal again. Fourth, how a meal remembers. The young Umar ibn Abi Salamah once ate with the Prophet, his hand wandering all over the dish.

teach.h: SAY GOD'S NAME, EAT WHAT'S NEAR.
teach.b: He was told: say God's name, eat with your right hand, and eat from what's in front of you.
Three small things, and a whole way of eating. In Mina the feast and the remembrance aren't separate. Someone passes the bread, and says bismillah as they take it.

how: In the days after Eid al-Adha, pilgrims stay in Mina, stone the pillars each afternoon, eat and drink, and say the takbir, and these days are not fasted.

games.q: what does “the days of tashriq” mean?
o: the first ten days of Dhul-Hijjah, before the Hajj
the feast days at Mina for eating and remembering God
the nights pilgrims spend sleeping at Muzdalifah

games.q: the days of tashriq — tap the pairs.
p: he stood long in du'a at the pillars
eat from what's in front of you

s: the Qur'an says leaving Mina early is a sin
whoever hurries off after two days, no sin; whoever stays, no sin.
the Qur'an tells pilgrims to remember God as they remembered their fathers, or more
Surah Al-Baqarah, after the rites are done.
the days of tashriq are days for fasting
the Prophet called them days of eating and drinking.

games.q: you're in Mina. two of the counted days have passed and your rites are done. do you stay or go?
o: you must stay to the end.
either: no sin if you hurry, no sin if you stay.
games.why: Surah Al-Baqarah gives both ways out, no sin either way, for the one who is mindful of God.

practice: Take something small, a date or a glass of water, or picture your next meal. If you pray, say bismillah before the first bite and alhamdulillah after; if not, pause and think of everyone it took to bring it to you.
Then eat slowly, with your right hand, from what's in front of you.

wordCard.voice: The days of tashriq. The days after the sacrifice, spent in Mina: days of eating, drinking, stoning the pillars and remembering God. Today's word.

orig.note: the days of tashriq, after the day of sacrifice.

carryVoice: Your line: eat and remember. At Mina, a meal is one more way of remembering. See you for the farewell.
